incidents.title: One client floods the public API
incidents.brief: A single API key sends 20,000 req/s and the shared cluster’s p99 jumps from 80ms to 4s.
incidents.constraint: Other tenants send 3,000 req/s in total and share the same edge and cluster.
incidents.question: What protects the majority of clients?

choices.label: Rate limit
choices.resultBody: Per-key rate limits at the edge so one caller cannot consume the whole fleet.

choices.label: More servers
choices.resultBody: New servers buy a few minutes, but nothing stops the single key's 20,000 req/s from filling them too; CPU stays at 100% and p95 reaches 1.1 s for every tenant.

nodes.sub: flood fills the new servers too
nodes.label: API (+4 servers)

choices.label: Longer timeouts
choices.resultBody: Longer timeouts keep queued requests alive, so the flood holds even more connections; other tenants now wait about 1 s instead of failing fast, and CPU stays pegged.

hints: One caller is starving the rest.
Unbounded QPS is the incident.
Cap by key at the edge.

knob.label: Per-key limit
knob.question: Set the per-key limit: the biggest honest key peaks at 1,200 req/s; p99 climbs past 8,000 total.

low.title: Honest tenants get throttled
low.body: Below 1,500 req/s the limit clips the biggest honest tenant's 1,200 req/s peaks and their bursts: at 1,000 its peak traffic gets 429s, and at 500 several paying tenants are throttled while the flood was already harmless.

high.title: The flood still fills the cluster
high.body: Above 4,500 req/s the noisy key keeps enough of its 20,000 req/s that, added to the other tenants' 3,000, total load passes the 8,000 req/s knee; CPU pins and p95 climbs back toward a second.

good.title: Flood capped, honest peaks fit
good.body: The noisy key is held to at most 4,500 req/s, so total load stays under about 7,500 req/s, below the 8,000 knee, while the biggest honest tenant's 1,200 req/s peak still fits with room for bursts. CPU settles between 36% and 70%.

incidents.title: Password guessing slips under the per-IP limit
incidents.brief: Attackers hit Nestbank's /login from 40k residential IPs, each under 1 attempt/min, guessing 60 passwords an hour against each of 20k accounts. The 10/min per-IP limit never fires.
incidents.constraint: Real customers must never be locked out by someone else's guesses.
incidents.question: What limit actually slows guessing on a targeted account?

choices.label: Per-account failure budget with backoff and CAPTCHA

tradeoffs.tradeoffSummary: Keys the limit on the target, not the source; known devices bypass the friction.

choices.resultBody: Failures are now counted per username across all IPs. After 5 in 15 minutes the account requires a CAPTCHA and each further failure doubles the delay, up to 15 minutes. Guesses per account fall from 60 to about 4 an hour, while the real owner on a known device cookie still signs in normally.

choices.label: Tighten the per-IP login limit from 10 to 2 per minute
choices.resultTitle: The botnet stays under any IP limit
choices.resultBody: Each attacking IP already sends less than 1 attempt a minute, so the tighter limit never fires on them. It does fire on office and mobile-carrier NATs, blocking 3% of real customers.

choices.label: Hard-lock the account for an hour after 5 failed attempts
choices.resultTitle: Attackers now lock out real customers
choices.resultBody: Guessing stops, but anyone can now lock any account with 5 bad passwords. The botnet re-locks all 20k targeted accounts every hour, and support takes 6,000 calls a day from customers who can't sign in.

hints: Count how many attempts each IP makes. Now count per account.
The attacker controls the source address, but not the target.
Friction that grows with failures hurts guessers more than owners.

variants.constraint: The application runs as an isolated single-node bastion where external Redis adds unnecessary network latency and failure modes.

rl2-memory.resultTitle: In-memory token bucket eliminates network overhead
rl2-memory.resultBody: For a standalone single-node bastion, an atomic local token bucket is faster, zero-cost, and has no network dependency.

rl2-redis.resultTitle: External Redis added an unnecessary point of failure
rl2-redis.resultBody: Provisioning a multi-node Redis cluster for a single server added network round-trips and cluster management cost without benefit.

incidents.title: Rate limit lets double traffic through at :00
incidents.brief: SMSly allows 600 messages per minute per account with a fixed window. A bulk sender fires 600 at 12:00:59 and 600 at 12:01:00; the carrier link, rated 20 msg/s, drops 40%.
incidents.constraint: Customers pay for 600/min on average and need short bursts of up to 50 messages.
incidents.question: Which limiter stops the window-edge double burst but still allows small bursts?

choices.label: Token bucket refilling 10/s with capacity 50

tradeoffs.tradeoffSummary: Smooth rate with an explicit burst allowance; big dumps take longer.

choices.resultBody: The bucket refills 10 tokens/s (600/min) and holds at most 50, so the worst burst is 50 messages then a steady 10/s; carrier drops fall from 40% to 0.5%. Cost: the 1,200-message dump now takes about 2 minutes, and each key stores a count and a timestamp.

choices.label: Shrink the fixed window to 100 messages per 10 s
choices.resultBody: The edge burst shrinks to 200 messages in about 2 s, 100 msg/s, still five times the carrier's 20 msg/s rating; drops only fall to 22%.

choices.label: Queue rejected messages and resend them each minute
choices.resultBody: Rejected messages pile up and are resent at the top of each minute, syncing the backlog into the same edge spike; drops stay at 38% and delivery lag grows to 4 minutes.

hints: The per-minute total is never exceeded.
Two full windows back to back put 1,200 messages into about 2 seconds.
Limit the rate continuously, with an explicit cap on burst size.

incidents.title: Five scripts hog the whole search cluster
incidents.brief: Queryly's full-text searches take 2-8 s each. Five analytics users run scripts that keep 40 searches each in flight, under the 60 req/min limit, holding 200 of the cluster's 240 search threads.
incidents.constraint: Search nodes are fixed until next quarter's budget.
incidents.question: What limit matches how search actually consumes capacity?

choices.label: Cap concurrent in-flight searches per user at 4

tradeoffs.tradeoffSummary: Limits occupancy instead of arrival rate; batch users trade speed for fairness.

choices.resultBody: Each user may now hold at most 4 running searches; extras wait in a per-user queue or get a 429. The five scripts drop from 200 threads to 20, leaving 220 for everyone else, and regular users' p95 falls from 14 s to 3 s. Cost: scripted exports take about ten times longer.

choices.label: Lower the search rate limit to 10 requests per minute
choices.resultTitle: Rate is fine; query duration is the problem
choices.resultBody: A per-minute limit ignores that one query can hold a thread for 8 s. The scripts switch to broader, slower queries and still hold 150 threads, while regular users firing quick type-ahead searches hit the lower cap and see 12% 429s.

choices.label: Put a 5-minute cache in front of search results
choices.resultBody: The analytics scripts page through unique queries, so the cache hit ratio is 4%. Threads stay pinned by the same five users and everyone else's p95 stays around 13 s.

hints: These users send few requests; each one is just very long.
Capacity here is threads held over time, not requests per minute.
What if you limited how many a user can have running at once?

incidents.title: Limit is 100 req/s, partner gets 2,400
incidents.brief: PayGrid caps each partner at 100 req/s, but the counter lives in memory on each of 24 gateway pods. One partner spreads evenly and gets 2,400 req/s through to the ledger.
incidents.constraint: Pods autoscale between 12 and 40; the limit must hold however many are running.
incidents.question: Where should the counter live so the limit is actually global?

choices.label: Atomic per-key counter in shared Redis for all pods

tradeoffs.tradeoffSummary: Global limit at the cost of a shared dependency on the hot path.

choices.resultBody: Every pod runs the same atomic INCR-with-expiry script on partner:{id}, so the 100 req/s cap holds at 24 or 40 pods and ledger CPU drops to 38%. Cost: a ~0.5 ms Redis round-trip per request, and a fail-open or fail-closed decision for Redis outages.

choices.label: Divide the limit by pod count, 4 req/s each
choices.resultBody: At 24 pods it roughly holds, but autoscaling to 40 lets 160 req/s through, and uneven balancing throttles the partner at 60 req/s on busy pods while others sit idle.

choices.label: Sticky-route each API key to a single gateway pod
choices.resultBody: The limit holds until the busiest partners pile onto a few pods; one hits 97% CPU, and every pod restart wipes its in-memory counters, briefly letting 2,400 req/s through again.

nodes.sub: big partners pinned to one pod

hints: Each pod enforces the limit correctly on its own.
24 pods each allowing 100 req/s is 2,400 req/s.
The pods need to agree on one count per key.

incidents.title: Throttled clients all come back at once
incidents.brief: Mapify returns 429 with no Retry-After, and its SDK retries immediately up to 5 times. When 8k req/s gets throttled, retries push the gateway to 40k req/s.
incidents.constraint: You own the server and ship SDK updates; there is no extra capacity this week.
incidents.question: What turns rejected requests into fewer requests, not more?

choices.label: Retry-After header plus SDK backoff with jitter

tradeoffs.tradeoffSummary: Server hints plus client discipline; depends on SDK adoption.

choices.resultBody: Each 429 now says Retry-After: 2, and the SDK waits 2, 4, then 8 s with full jitter, so retry load drops from 32k to about 3k req/s and rejections fall from 72% to 9%. Cost: throttled calls finish seconds later, and old SDK versions keep hammering until upgraded.

choices.label: Return 503 instead of 429 for throttled calls
choices.resultBody: Many HTTP clients and proxies treat 503 as a transient server fault and retry it automatically, so gateway traffic climbs to 46k req/s and dashboards now report an outage.

choices.label: Cut the SDK's retry cap from 5 attempts to 1
choices.resultBody: Retry volume shrinks, but the single retry still fires instantly and in lockstep, so each throttle wave doubles traffic; rejections only fall from 72% to 55%.

hints: Most of the 40k req/s are not new requests.
Clients retry instantly and all at the same moment.
Tell clients when to come back, and make them spread out.

incidents.title: Gold partner gets 429s while free tier floods
incidents.brief: Formly's API has one cluster-wide limit of 50k req/s. A free-tier scraping wave takes 46k of it, and the gold partner's 3k req/s of SLA traffic gets 429s 35% of the time.
incidents.constraint: Gold contracts guarantee 5k req/s; the free tier must keep working, just slower.
incidents.question: What guarantees each tier its share of the 50k req/s capacity?

choices.label: Per-tenant token buckets with a reserved gold quota

tradeoffs.tradeoffSummary: Isolation between tenants; quotas must be sized and maintained.

choices.resultBody: Gold keys draw from a reserved 5k req/s bucket, and free keys share the other 45k with a 200 req/s per-key cap; gold rejections fall from 35% to 0.2%. Cost: a tier lookup on every request, per-contract quotas to maintain, and scrapers now see 429s.

choices.label: Raise the cluster-wide limit to 80k req/s
choices.resultBody: The free-tier wave grows into the new headroom, API CPU hits 99% and p95 climbs to 2.1 s; gold is rarely 429ed now, but 20% of its calls time out instead.

choices.label: Prioritize gold requests in the API's work queue
choices.resultBody: Requests are reordered only after the gateway admits them, and the 46k free req/s still saturate workers; gold waits less, but 18% of its calls still miss the 1 s deadline.

hints: A limit exists; everyone just shares it.
One tier is spending capacity promised to another.
Give each tenant its own budget instead of one global one.

incidents.title: One GraphQL call does 4,000 DB lookups
incidents.brief: Shoplane's GraphQL API allows 100 requests/min per key. A scraper packs 200 aliased product queries with nested reviews into each request, costing 4,000 DB lookups apiece; catalog DB CPU hits 96%.
incidents.constraint: The public schema and existing client apps cannot change.
incidents.question: What should the limiter count for a GraphQL request?

choices.label: Score query cost at parse time; budget points per key

tradeoffs.tradeoffSummary: Limits the work a request asks for, not the number of HTTP calls.

choices.resultBody: Before execution the server walks the parsed query and multiplies field costs by requested list sizes, so 200 aliases with nested reviews score about 4,000 points against a 10,000-point-per-minute budget. The scraper gets 2 such calls a minute instead of 100; normal app queries score under 50 and never notice. Cost: every field needs a cost annotation.

choices.label: Reject any GraphQL request with more than 20 aliases
choices.resultTitle: The scraper just splits its requests
choices.resultBody: The scraper sends 10 requests of 20 aliases each, still under 100 a minute, and nested connections still fan out. DB CPU falls only to 90%, and legitimate dashboards that batch 30 widgets per call break.

choices.label: Lower the per-key limit to 10 requests per minute
choices.resultTitle: Normal clients choke, the scraper doesn't
choices.resultBody: Each scraper call still carries 4,000 lookups, and the scraper simply adds more keys. Meanwhile the mobile app, which makes 30 small queries per screen, starts getting 429s on 18% of requests.

hints: In GraphQL, one HTTP request can ask for almost anything.
The server knows how expensive a query is before running it.
Charge requests for the work they ask for, not for arriving.

incidents.title: Partner webhook retries triple our traffic
incidents.brief: Paylink's partner sends 400 payment webhooks/s during a sale. The handler writes synchronously to a DB that takes 150/s; timeouts return 500, and the partner retries any non-2xx within 1 s.
incidents.constraint: The partner ignores Retry-After, and no event may be dropped.
incidents.question: How do you absorb the burst without triggering more retries?

choices.label: Ack into a durable queue, drain to the DB at 150/s

tradeoffs.tradeoffSummary: Shapes bursts into a steady rate at the cost of processing delay.

choices.resultTitle: Retries stop and the backlog drains
choices.resultBody: The handler verifies the signature, appends to a durable queue, and returns 202 in 5 ms, so the partner stops retrying and inbound falls back to 400/s. Workers drain at a steady 150/s, the DB's safe rate, and the sale backlog clears about 25 minutes after the peak. Cost: events apply minutes late, so consumers must tolerate delay and duplicates.

choices.label: Return 429 whenever the handler exceeds 150 events per second
choices.resultBody: The partner treats every non-2xx as a failure and retries within a second, so rejected events come straight back and inbound stays near 1,100/s. Events that exceed the partner's 5-retry cap are dropped for good.

choices.label: Grow the handler pool from 50 to 400 threads
choices.resultBody: More concurrent writers only pile onto a DB that tops out at 150 writes/s. Lock waits push each write past the 10 s timeout, errors rise to 75%, and retries push inbound to 1,500/s.

hints: Every slow or failed answer comes back as another request.
The partner is happy the moment you say 2xx.
Accepting an event and processing it don't have to happen at the same rate.

incidents.title: Backfill job crowds out paying customers
incidents.brief: Ledgr's backfill calls the public API at 9k req/s beside 6k req/s of interactive traffic. The cluster tops out at 12k req/s, so customers see 25% errors during APAC business hours.
incidents.constraint: The backfill must finish within 24 hours, and customers are in every time zone.
incidents.question: Under overload, whose requests should be dropped first?

choices.label: Mark backfill sheddable; drop it first under overload

tradeoffs.tradeoffSummary: Priority shedding: batch work uses spare capacity and yields under pressure.

choices.resultTitle: Customers stay fast, the backfill soaks up slack
choices.resultBody: Requests now carry a criticality header. When cluster concurrency passes 85%, the gateway rejects sheddable calls with 429 before any interactive call is touched. Interactive errors fall to 0.1% and the backfill runs on the remaining headroom, about 6k req/s, finishing in 19 hours. Cost: the job must back off and resume from checkpoints.

choices.label: Only run the backfill between 01:00 and 05:00 UTC
choices.resultBody: The quiet window for Europe is business hours in Singapore and Sydney, so interactive load there peaks at the same time. Errors still hit 18%, and a 4-hour window means the backfill now needs 6 days.

choices.label: Give the backfill a fixed 6k req/s quota
choices.resultTitle: A fixed quota ignores current load
choices.resultBody: With interactive traffic at 6k the total sits exactly at the 12k ceiling, and every spike tips it over. Errors drop from 25% to 9%, and at quiet times the job idles while spare capacity goes unused.

hints: Not every request is equally urgent.
A batch job can wait an hour; a customer at checkout can't.
Let the system know which requests it may drop when it's full.

incidents.title: Scalper gets double the ticket limit
incidents.brief: Tixly's 6 gateways share Redis counters keyed by each gateway's local minute. One VM's clock drifted 40 s after a host migration, so its requests land in another window key and a scalper gets 2x the 300/min limit.
incidents.constraint: Hosts migrate weekly; clock drift can come back at any time.
incidents.question: Where should the rate window's notion of time come from?

choices.label: Pick window keys in a Lua script using Redis TIME

tradeoffs.tradeoffSummary: A single time source for counting; gateway clocks no longer matter.

choices.resultBody: The limiter's Lua script now calls TIME on Redis to pick the window, so all six gateways count against the same window no matter what their own clocks say. The scalper is back to 300 a minute. Cost: a Redis failover can shift window boundaries once by the new primary's clock offset.

choices.label: Alert on NTP drift and restart any skewed gateway VM
choices.resultTitle: Drifted VM restarted, limit back near 300
choices.resultBody: The alert caught gateway 6 and the restart resynced its clock, so the scalper is back to about 330 a minute. The alert only fires after 5 s of skew, though, and the next weekly host migration is on Tuesday.

choices.label: Widen the limiter window from 1 minute to 10 minutes
choices.resultTitle: The whole limit can be spent in one burst
choices.resultBody: A 40 s skew now splits the count only near window edges, but the limit becomes 3,000 per 10 minutes, so a bot can buy 3,000 tickets in the first seconds of a sale. The next release sells out to scalpers in 12 s.

hints: The counter is shared, but the clocks that name the window are not.
Six machines means six opinions about which minute it is.
Let the store that holds the counters also decide what time it is.

incidents.title: Bots brute-force SMS login codes
incidents.brief: Walleto's 6-digit SMS codes stay valid 30 minutes, and its limiter only counts successful checks. A bot spread across 50 sessions tries 60k codes/min and cracks a code in about 8 minutes.
incidents.constraint: Users on slow SMS delivery need codes to stay valid for minutes, not seconds.
incidents.question: How do you make guessing a code hopeless?

choices.label: Count every attempt first; burn the code after 5 misses

tradeoffs.tradeoffSummary: Limit is keyed on the secret being guessed, so rotating sessions doesn't help.

choices.resultBody: Every verification now increments a counter keyed on the code itself before checking, and the fifth miss invalidates the code and forces a new SMS. A bot's odds per code drop to 5 in a million, so hijacks stop, while a user who mistypes still gets four more tries. Cost: code resends need their own limit.

choices.label: Count failed checks per session with a 10-per-minute cap
choices.resultBody: The limit is keyed on the session, which the bot creates for free. It opens 6,000 fresh sessions a minute and keeps guessing at the same rate against the same code, so hijacks barely move.

choices.label: Shorten the SMS code lifetime from 30 minutes to 5 minutes
choices.resultBody: At 60k guesses a minute the bot still tries 300k codes in 5 minutes, about a 30% chance per code. Hijacks fall only by half, and users with slow SMS delivery now see 6% expired codes.

hints: Failed guesses are free right now. That's the whole attack.
A limit keyed on something the attacker can mint is no limit.
Tie the budget to the one code being guessed.

incidents.title: Every reader at one POP gets 'Too Many Requests'
incidents.brief: Newsly's limiter returns 429 to one heavy client, and a default Cache-Control: public, max-age=60 header lets the CDN cache that 429 on the article URL. For a minute, 40k readers at that POP get throttled.
incidents.constraint: Articles must stay CDN-cached with a 60 s TTL.
incidents.question: How do you keep one client's 429 from reaching everyone?

choices.label: Send 429s with Cache-Control: no-store and Retry-After

tradeoffs.tradeoffSummary: Error responses are never shared; successful pages stay cached.

choices.resultBody: The limiter now overrides the default header on every 429 with no-store, so the CDN passes it through without caching it, and Retry-After tells the heavy client when to return. Readers at that POP get the cached article again and hit ratio stays at 96%. Cost: throttled calls still travel to the origin limiter.

choices.label: Lower the CDN TTL for all article pages from 60 s to 5 s
choices.resultTitle: Shorter outages, much lower hit ratio
choices.resultBody: A cached 429 now lasts 5 s instead of 60 s, but it still hits everyone at the POP each time the heavy client trips the limit. Hit ratio falls to 71%, pushing 10k more req/s to origin.

choices.label: Return 200 with an error JSON body instead of 429
choices.resultTitle: The CDN caches the error as a success
choices.resultBody: A 200 with the default public header is cached exactly like an article, so every reader at that POP gets the error body for the full 60 s, and clients no longer know to back off. Reader errors rise to 45%.

hints: The 429 is right for one client and wrong for everyone else.
A shared cache stores whatever a response says it may store.
What header keeps a response out of every shared cache?

incidents.title: One WebSocket floods a 50k-member channel
incidents.brief: Chatterly limits HTTP to 20 req/s per user, but a bot opens one WebSocket and sends 10,000 messages/s into a 50k-member channel. Fanout workers hit 99% CPU and delivery lags 40 s for everyone.
incidents.constraint: Real users burst up to 5 messages per second when pasting.
incidents.question: Where should the message limit be enforced?

choices.label: Per-connection message bucket in the WebSocket gateway

tradeoffs.tradeoffSummary: Limits the message stream itself, not just connection setup.

choices.resultTitle: The flood stops at the socket
choices.resultBody: Each connection gets a bucket of 10 messages refilled at 3 per second. Excess frames are dropped with a warning, and a socket over the limit for 30 s is closed. The bot is down to 3 msg/s, fanout CPU falls to 45% and delivery lag to 200 ms, while pasting bursts still fit. Cost: about 50 bytes of state per socket.

choices.label: Limit new WebSocket connections to 5 per minute per IP
choices.resultTitle: One connection is all it needs
choices.resultBody: The bot only needs a single long-lived socket, so a connection-rate limit never fires. 10,000 messages a second keep flowing and delivery lag stays at 40 s.

choices.label: Throttle sends to 3 per second in the official clients
choices.resultTitle: Bots don't run your client code
choices.resultBody: The web and mobile apps now behave, but the bot speaks the raw WebSocket protocol and ignores client code entirely. The flood continues unchanged, and legitimate paste bursts start getting delayed.

hints: The HTTP limiter never sees these messages.
One connection can carry unlimited traffic after the handshake.
Enforce limits at the server that reads each frame.

incidents.title: Two modded clients lag a 64-player match
incidents.brief: Arenaforge match servers simulate 64 players at 60 Hz. Two modded clients send 900 input packets/s each instead of 60, and the server processes every one, stretching ticks to 40 ms; everyone rubber-bands.
incidents.constraint: Legit clients may burst to 120 packets/s after a reconnect.
incidents.question: How do you stop two players from lagging the whole match?

choices.label: Per-player packet budget, excess dropped before the tick

tradeoffs.tradeoffSummary: Fair share per player; nobody's input can starve the tick.

choices.resultBody: Each player gets a token bucket of 60 packets per second with a burst of 120, checked on the network thread. Excess packets are dropped before reaching the simulation, and repeat offenders get flagged for anti-cheat. Tick time falls to 9 ms and CPU to 55%. Cost: an honest burst beyond 120 loses a few inputs.

choices.label: Queue every input packet and process them as ticks allow
choices.resultBody: Nothing is dropped, but the queue grows by about 1,700 packets every second. Honest players' inputs wait behind the modded ones, input delay climbs to 2 s, and memory grows until the server crashes.

choices.label: Raise player disconnect timeouts from 5 s to 20 s to stop kicks
choices.resultBody: Players stop getting kicked, but ticks still take 40 ms, so the match runs in slow motion and keeps rubber-banding. More people now stay connected to a broken match.

hints: The server does work for every packet, no matter who sent it.
A 60 Hz game needs only about 60 inputs per second per player.
Decide which packets deserve simulation before simulating them.

incidents.title: Whole campus blocked during exam week
incidents.brief: Studyhub limits 300 req/min per IP. During exams, 4,000 students at one university share a single NAT address and 92% of their requests get 429, while a scraper on 200 cloud IPs sails through.
incidents.constraint: Anonymous visitors, about 20% of traffic, must still be limited somehow.
incidents.question: What should the limit be keyed on?

choices.label: Key limits on account ID, with a loose per-IP ceiling

tradeoffs.tradeoffSummary: Identity-based limits; IP only as a coarse backstop for anonymous traffic.

choices.resultTitle: Each student gets their own budget
choices.resultBody: Signed-in traffic, 80% of requests, is now limited per account at 300 a minute, so each student has a separate budget. Anonymous requests keep a per-IP limit raised to 5,000 a minute so shared NATs aren't punished. Campus 429s drop from 92% to 0.3%. Cost: scrapers must be caught by per-account limits and signup friction instead.

choices.label: Allowlist the university's NAT address from rate limits
choices.resultTitle: Unlimited campus, until someone abuses it
choices.resultBody: The campus is unblocked, but that IP now has no limit at all. A student's scraping script in the dorms sends 8k req/s unthrottled, and the next campus to complain needs another manual allowlist entry.

choices.label: Raise the per-IP limit to 20,000 requests per minute
choices.resultTitle: Every IP gets a huge budget
choices.resultBody: The campus fits, but so does every single-user IP, including each of the scraper's 200 cloud addresses. Scraper traffic jumps to 60k req/s and origin CPU hits 95%.

hints: One IP address is not one person.
Most of this traffic arrives already signed in.
Limit the identity you actually trust, and keep IP as a backstop.

incidents.title: AMA thread generates 8M notification writes/s
incidents.brief: On Buzzboard, every comment notifies each thread subscriber. A 200k-subscriber AMA gets 40 comments/s, creating 8M notification writes/s; the notification DB saturates and pushes arrive 20 minutes late platform-wide.
incidents.constraint: AMA commenters must not be throttled; it's the main event.
incidents.question: What should be limited: the comments, or what they cause?

choices.label: Coalesce alerts into one digest per subscriber per minute

tradeoffs.tradeoffSummary: Limits the amplified side effect, not the user action.

choices.resultTitle: One write per subscriber per minute
choices.resultBody: Instead of one notification per comment, each subscriber gets at most one '37 new replies' notification per thread per minute, upserted in place. Writes for the AMA fall from 8M/s to about 3.3k/s, the DB recovers, and push lag drops to 5 s. Cost: subscribers see new replies up to a minute later.

choices.label: Limit each user to 5 comments per minute in the thread
choices.resultBody: Almost nobody posts more than 5 comments a minute; the 40 comments/s come from about 2,000 different people. Volume barely changes and notification writes stay near 7.5M/s.

choices.label: Shard the notification database 10 more ways by user ID
choices.resultTitle: Shards fill as fast as you add them
choices.resultBody: Capacity rises from 1M to 3M writes/s, still far below 8M, for $18k a month more. Push lag falls only to 12 minutes, and the next bigger AMA takes it down again.

hints: 40 requests per second is not the problem.
Each comment multiplies into 200k writes downstream.
Does a subscriber need one alert per reply, or one per burst of replies?

incidents.title: Everyone gets 429 after the load balancer move
incidents.brief: After Parcelo moved to a new L7 load balancer, its 100 req/s per-IP limiter keys on the socket peer address, now one of 4 LB IPs. All 30k req/s look like 4 clients; 97% get 429.
incidents.constraint: Clients can send any X-Forwarded-For value they like.
incidents.question: Which address should the limiter key on?

choices.label: Key on the X-Forwarded-For entry the trusted LB appended

tradeoffs.tradeoffSummary: Correct client identity through proxies, without trusting client headers.

choices.resultTitle: Each client gets its own bucket again
choices.resultBody: The limiter now reads X-Forwarded-For from the right and takes the entry added by the trusted LB, ignoring anything the client could have forged. Traffic spreads back across 120k real IPs and 429s drop to 0.2%, all from actual abusers. Cost: the LB's address ranges must stay in the trusted-proxy config.

choices.label: Key on the first, leftmost address in X-Forwarded-For
choices.resultBody: The leftmost value is whatever the client sent, so abusers put a random address in every request and get a fresh bucket each time. Legitimate 429s disappear, and so does all protection: one scraper reaches 12k req/s.

choices.label: Raise the per-IP limit from 100 to 10,000 req/s
choices.resultTitle: Four giant buckets and no real limit
choices.resultBody: Each LB address can now carry 10k req/s, so real users pass, but the limiter is effectively off. A single abuser can take a whole LB address's budget and pushes the origin to 94% CPU.

hints: Nothing about the users changed; the network path did.
The limiter only sees whoever opened the TCP connection to it.
A proxy you trust records the real client. A client can write anything.

incidents.title: Static limit admits traffic a failing DB can't serve
incidents.brief: Rentora's API has a static 5,000 req/s limit, tuned while the database was healthy. During a DB failover capacity drops to 2,000 req/s, the limiter still admits 5,000, and p99 climbs from 120 ms to 30 s.
incidents.constraint: Real capacity shifts with DB health, cache warmth, and deploys.
incidents.question: How should the limit track what the system can handle right now?

choices.label: Adaptive concurrency limit that shrinks as latency rises

tradeoffs.tradeoffSummary: Limit is measured continuously instead of guessed once.

choices.resultBody: The gateway now tracks in-flight requests against latency: when p99 rises above the no-load baseline it cuts the concurrency limit, and it probes upward as latency recovers. During failover it settles at roughly 2,000 req/s; excess gets fast 503s and admitted requests keep a p99 of 300 ms. Cost: smoothing needs tuning to avoid oscillation.

choices.label: Lower the static limit from 5,000 to 2,000 req/s permanently
choices.resultTitle: Safe in failover, wasteful the rest of the time
choices.resultBody: Failovers no longer melt the API, but on normal days the system could serve 5,000 req/s and now rejects 45% of peak traffic with 429s. Revenue drops every evening to protect against a few minutes a month.

choices.label: Increase the gateway request timeout from 5 s to 30 s
choices.resultTitle: Requests wait longer, then fail anyway
choices.resultBody: Longer timeouts keep more requests in flight, so queues grow deeper, memory climbs, and p99 sits at the new 30 s ceiling. Clients retry the timed-out calls, adding 40% more load to a struggling database.

hints: The limit was right, for a system that no longer exists.
Rising latency is the earliest sign that capacity has dropped.
What if the limit were recomputed from what the system is doing now?

incidents.title: Every pod runs the midnight sync at once
incidents.brief: Stockr's sync cron runs in all 30 pods at 00:00, each calling a supplier API at 50 req/s. The supplier allows 50 req/s per account; 1,500 req/s earns 429s, and after 1,000 it suspends our key for 24 h.
incidents.constraint: Pods autoscale between 10 and 60.
incidents.question: How do you keep outbound calls within the supplier's limit?

choices.label: One leased job runner with a shared 50 req/s bucket

tradeoffs.tradeoffSummary: One runner and one outbound budget, independent of scaling.

choices.resultTitle: Exactly one sync, under the supplier's cap
choices.resultBody: Pods race for a Redis lease at 00:00 and only the winner runs the sync. Every outbound supplier call, including ad-hoc ones from other pods, takes a token from one shared bucket refilling at 45 req/s for headroom. 429s drop to 0 and the key stays active at any pod count. Cost: the sync takes 15 minutes instead of 30 s.

choices.label: Add random 0-60 s jitter to each pod's cron start
choices.resultTitle: Spread out, still 30 times the calls
choices.resultBody: Starts are staggered, but 30 pods still each run the full sync, so overlapping jobs push 700-1,500 req/s at the supplier. 429s keep piling up and the key is suspended by 00:04.

choices.label: Cap each pod at 50 supplier calls per second
choices.resultTitle: Per-pod limits multiply with pod count
choices.resultBody: Every pod is polite on its own, but 30 pods at 50 req/s is still 1,500 req/s, and autoscaling to 60 pods doubles it. The key is suspended within 2 minutes.

hints: The supplier sees one account, not 30 pods.
Thirty copies of a job means thirty times the calls, however they are spaced.
Both the job and the outbound budget need to exist exactly once.

incidents.title: Rejected requests still melt the session database
incidents.brief: StreamBox's limiter runs inside the video API, after session lookup. A credential-stuffing botnet sends 90k req/s; 87% get 429, but each still costs a session-DB query.
incidents.constraint: Legitimate traffic is 12k req/s, and the session DB cannot be scaled up this quarter.
incidents.question: Where should the throttle run so rejected traffic is cheap?

choices.label: Per-IP and per-key token buckets at the edge

tradeoffs.tradeoffSummary: Cheap coarse rejection at the edge, fine-grained rules stay in the service.

choices.resultBody: The edge now rejects about 78k abusive req/s before they reach the origin or the session DB, so DB CPU drops from 97% to 31%. Cost: the edge only knows IPs and API keys, so per-user rules still need a finer limiter inside the API.

choices.label: Cache session lookups in the API process for 60 s
choices.resultBody: The botnet cycles random credentials, so nearly every lookup misses the cache; DB CPU only falls to 91%, and revoked sessions now stay valid for up to 60 s.

choices.label: Lower the in-API limiter from 100 to 20 req/s
choices.resultBody: More requests get 429, but every one is still rejected after its session query; DB CPU stays at 96%, and legitimate households sharing an IP are now throttled too.

hints: The limiter is doing its job: most requests are rejected.
Every rejection still pays for a database query first.
Move the rejection ahead of the expensive work.

culprit.explanation: The Video API logs show every 429 is decided after auth.loadSession() has already queried the session DB, so each rejected bot request still costs a lookup. The DB is only the victim.

wrongNodeFeedback.sess: The session DB is drowning, but it is only answering the queries it is sent. Look at what decides to send a query for a request that is about to be rejected.
wrongNodeFeedback.edge: The edge forwards everything because nobody asked it to limit; it is not broken. Find where the 429 is actually decided.
wrongNodeFeedback.gw: The gateway passes traffic through untouched. The expensive work happens further in.
wrongNodeFeedback.bots: The botnet is the trigger, not the fault: an attack like this is expected. What makes each rejected request so costly?

api: 78k 429/s, each preceded by a session query
sess: slow: SELECT * FROM sessions WHERE token=$1 (2.1 s)

incidents.title: Gateway heap climbs until GC stalls every request
incidents.brief: Gatekeep's limiter keeps per-IP counters in an in-process map that never evicts. Rotating-IP scanners add 2M keys an hour; after 8 h heaps hit 95% and GC pushes p99 to 900 ms.
incidents.constraint: A bounded-LRU fix is in review and ships Thursday; nothing else risky may deploy before Friday's sale.
incidents.question: What keeps the gateways healthy until the fix lands?

choices.label: Rolling restart of the gateways every 6 h until Thursday

tradeoffs.tradeoffSummary: Heap never reaches the GC cliff; each restart resets that pod's counters for one window.

choices.resultTitle: Heaps reset before GC can bite
choices.resultBody: A scheduled job drains and restarts one gateway at a time every 6 hours, so heaps peak near 55% and p99 falls back to 70 ms. Cost: each restarted pod forgets its counters, letting a client get up to one extra minute's quota.

choices.label: Move every limiter counter into a new Redis Cluster today
choices.resultBody: A new client library, a cluster, load tests and a cutover do not fit in a day. The rushed deploy ships with the old map still populated as a fallback, so heaps keep climbing, and it breaks the no-risky-deploys rule.

choices.label: Swap the counter map for a count-min sketch on each gateway
choices.resultBody: The hurried sketch has fixed memory, but it is sized for 100k keys and 2M rotating IPs collide constantly. Its overcounting throttles 4% of legitimate clients, and it is an untested limiter rewrite shipped days before the sale.

hints: The real fix already exists; it just is not live yet.
The heap is fine right after a pod starts and degrades over hours.
What resets an unbounded in-memory map without shipping new code?

incidents.title: Limiter's Redis blips and every partner gets 429
incidents.brief: The shared Redis limiter failed over for 25 s during payroll. The limiter fails closed on errors, so all 24 gateway pods returned 429 to every partner and 2,400 payouts failed.
incidents.constraint: The ledger survives at most 600 req/s, and Redis failovers happen a few times a month.
incidents.question: How should the limiter behave when Redis is unreachable?

choices.label: On Redis errors, fall back to local per-pod buckets

tradeoffs.tradeoffSummary: Degrade to an approximate local limit instead of choosing between no limit and no service.

choices.resultBody: When a Redis call fails, each pod switches to an in-memory bucket of the limit divided by pod count, about 4 req/s per partner at 24 pods, and returns to the shared counter when Redis recovers. The 25 s blip admits roughly the contracted rate, far under the ledger's 600 req/s. Cost: the limit is approximate during a failover.

choices.label: Fail open and skip rate limiting while Redis is down
choices.resultBody: Payouts continue, but the partners' retry backlog floods in unthrottled: 2,400 req/s hit a ledger that survives 600, it pins at 99% CPU, and the ledger outage outlasts the Redis blip it was meant to ride through.

choices.label: Retry each failed Redis call three times before rejecting
choices.resultTitle: Slow rejections instead of fast ones
choices.resultBody: Every request now waits through three timed-out attempts, about 1.5 s, before being rejected anyway. Gateway threads pile up, p99 hits 2 s for every partner, and the 25 s blip still fails nearly every payout.

hints: The limiter has to decide something when its counter store is gone.
Rejecting everything and admitting everything both break a promise.
An approximate limit is better than no limit or no service for 25 seconds.

incidents.title: Bots pump SMS codes to premium numbers
incidents.brief: Code-burning stopped the guessing, so the bots switched: they request fresh codes nonstop, 40k SMS an hour to premium-rate numbers they own. The SMS bill hit $6,000 today.
incidents.constraint: Real users sometimes need two or three resends when delivery is slow.
incidents.question: What limit stops the SMS flood without stranding real users?

choices.label: Limit resends per phone number with growing cooldowns

tradeoffs.tradeoffSummary: Key the limit on the costly resource, the destination number, not the session asking.

choices.resultBody: Each number now gets at most 3 codes an hour, with cooldowns of 30 s, 2 minutes and then 10 minutes, and premium-rate number ranges are refused outright. SMS volume falls from 40k to about 900 an hour, while a real user still gets two resends. Cost: a number lookup before each send.

choices.label: Put a CAPTCHA in front of every code verification attempt
choices.resultTitle: The money is spent at send time
choices.resultBody: The CAPTCHA guards verification, but the cost is paid when a code is sent. The bots never verify anything, so 40k SMS an hour keep flowing and the bill keeps climbing.

choices.label: Cap total SMS sends platform-wide at 5,000 per hour
choices.resultTitle: Bots spend the whole hourly cap
choices.resultBody: The bill is capped, but the bots use all 5,000 sends in the first ten minutes of each hour, so real users get no code at all for fifty minutes of every hour.

hints: The bots no longer want to log in; they want you to send messages.
Money is spent at the moment a code is sent, not when it is checked.
Limit the scarce thing per destination, and keep a little room for honest resends.

incidents.title: Scalpers double the limit again during an on-sale
incidents.brief: The NTP alert fixed gateway 6, until Tuesday's host migration drifted gateways 2 and 4 by 30 s during a stadium on-sale. The alert fired after 6 minutes; scalpers bought 22% of tickets.
incidents.constraint: Hosts migrate weekly; the 300 per minute limit must hold whatever a gateway's clock says.
incidents.question: What takes gateway clocks out of the limiter entirely?

choices.label: Key counters by user alone and let Redis EXPIRE end windows

tradeoffs.tradeoffSummary: One clock, Redis's own expiry, defines every window; gateway time never enters the key.

choices.resultBody: The first request in a window runs INCR on user:{id} and sets a 60 s EXPIRE, so the window is timed by Redis and no gateway clock appears in the key. The scalper is held to 300 a minute through any drift. Cost: each user's window starts at their first request, so edges differ per user.

choices.label: Tighten the NTP drift alert from 5 s down to 1 s of skew
choices.resultBody: The alert now fires within a minute of a migration, but it still reacts only after drift exists, each restart takes 10 minutes, and harmless 1 s blips page twice a day. Scalpers still get about 1.4x the limit during every migration.

choices.label: Opt the six gateway VMs out of live host migration entirely
choices.resultBody: The cloud still performs forced maintenance: VMs that cannot live-migrate are stopped and restarted, so gateways vanish for 3 minutes each week and come back with unsynced clocks anyway.

hints: The alert can only react to drift that has already happened.
The window key is built from each gateway's own clock.
Let the one shared store decide when a window ends.
